source_text: I think running 象 on agent turns will find a LOT of promises, but agents tend to be very reactive, and sometimes they will promise things only to be overriden and redirected by me in the next turn (whether rightly or wrongly, often until we converge to something).  I don't think I'd base the model agent on agent prose right now because it's a bit too frothy.  I think it would be better to be more explicit at first, you think it would be better to run the annotation command on the agent speech... How about we meet in the middle and just look at  the current *claude-repl:claude-1* session, from line 6706 or so.  On that line I am responding to learning that claude-1 was being very inefficient.  Later in the session I learned that not only were they being inefficient with managing a development process, yet again, they had been building things that I didn't want and NOT building things that I did want.  My sense is that if I wanted to make the overall process work better, I wouldn't look for promises that were made in the REPL, but for a much more structured build process that would have been running on a pace of months.  (Maybe the tools would have made it more efficient.)

reply_text:
Gist: I read that stretch of the claude-1 session, and it supports your view: what went wrong was not broken REPL promises but standing requirements of yours that were never held anywhere the build had to check.

I read your 41 turns from line 6706 to the end, and only skimmed claude-1's replies.

**What claude-1's prose promises look like**
- There are about 54 lines of the "I'll…" kind. Of the 25 I read, most are procedural and short-lived: "I'll report when it lands", nearly always beside a job id and a park.
- So the promises that matter there are already recorded as parks. Reading the prose would add froth, as you expected, and would not have caught any of the failures.

**What the failures were**
- In about ten of your 41 turns you say a requirement was already stated: "I already told you this above", "time and time again", "repeated 100 times", "violating my core design from the first step".
- Two were countable and nobody counted them: three missions on a whitelist, and a policy space with one member across 20 clicks.
- One was about what got built: a per-target loader and a "thin path" you did not want, while the debugger and the forward-running machine you did want were not built.

**What that means in Elephant terms**
The commitments that were broken are yours to the program, not the agent's to you: requirements the program must keep satisfying. McCarthy's version is a rule stated over history and checked against every new act. Two things follow:
- 象 already reads the right side. Your turns are where the requirements are stated.
- What is missing is a register of them that outlives a session, each with a check that can be run.

**What a structured process would hold**
- Each requirement, with the turn where you stated it.
- Where possible, a number that can be counted from a run: missions in the field, policies compared, tasks handed to authors.
- The three states from the live-gap work: open, asserted by an agent, closed by a record fresher than the assertion.
- A check before each run that refuses to start when a counted number is degenerate.

claude-1 began this today in the PROOF-2b actions draft, as a numbered list of your rulings. It covers today only.

**A middle step I could take**
Take the rulings in that draft and search the 4,649 analysed operator turns back to 22 August for earlier statements of each. That would give a date each requirement was first stated and how many times it was repeated before being acted on. It uses only your turns and no agent prose.

On the Kimi/Zai harness: I agree it is the place to pilot a declared act if one is needed, and nothing in this stretch calls for one yet.

Shall I run that search?
